task.goal: Write the life this cycle's record produced. Lead with a named interviewed person or a Packet-named place. The feed or tracker line is the weather, never the lede.

task.approach: Voices approach: this slice is a roster, a tip sheet, not your assignment — every citizen with a page on the record, one line each. You pick whose own words carry the day, and why. The person's own line first, before their name; then who they are in one plain clause; then what in the city they were answering, from the page's own tags. Fewer, longer passages; the words are the product. Never a count, never a statistic, never an explanation of what they meant. Facts on this slice: the names, places, roles and numbers listed. Those are real; do not invent people or places. Everything else about this beat — what it looks like, who is there, what they want and hate — is yours to paint.

sources.name: Ximena Mehta
sources.quote: The A's success is all anyone can talk about around here. I mean, I'm a huge fan, and my husband Deacon is too. We plan our whole schedule around the games.

sources.name: Priya Narang
sources.quote: The A's winning season really brings Uptown together. When they're doing well, the whole neighborhood feels it. The bars and galleries stay packed, and you can feel the energy. It's like we're all connected then.

sources.name: Omar Amici
sources.quote: To be honest, the changes in Uptown have me feeling a bit uneasy. The streets are busier than ever, and it seems like every other place is a for-rent sign these days. I've lived here long enough to see the neighborhood transform, but this feels different. It's like the neighborhood is shifting away from the people who've been here all along.

sources.name: Dax Monroe
sources.quote: I've been thinking a lot about the cycles of life in Rockridge lately. The other night, I was at the window, just observing the world go by. It made me reflect on how people's lives are intertwined with the events around them. I've seen it in my own life, with my kids growing up and the community changing.

“"Yeah, it’s like the lake knows when you need it most. I’ve been walking the lakeside path more lately, especially when the mornings are quiet. It’s funny how the same water can feel so different depending on the day or the light." "Funny you say that—I was just watching the sunset from the pergola yesterday, thinking how the light turns everything gold for about five perfect minutes. Makes me wish I’d brought my camera, but maybe some things are just meant to be remembered, not captured." "I think that’s why I keep coming back to the lake path, even when I’m tired after work. It’s those unexpected moments—like when the herons decide to put on a show, or you catch neighbors laughing by the bandstand. Makes the whole city feel connected."” — Ximena Mehta, Bart Transit PR, Lake Merritt (own page, in conversation, C108)

“I should’ve pushed harder for those safety regs at the warehouse. Deacon’s hand wouldn’t be rotting in a biohazard bin if management gave half a damn about gloves that actually fit. Maurice was coughing blood by the time 23 got to him—should’ve called that in sooner. And Ariana... fuck. I read her chart again today like the numbers would change. They never do. --- Yu Zen makes the third warehouse injury this month. Third. And every damn incident report says the same thing: "Employee failed to follow protocol." Like it's always the worker's fault, never the shitty equipment. Deacon's hand was black by the time he hit the OR. I keep seeing his wife's face in triage—like she already knew, just waiting for us to say it out loud. Ariana’s chart’s still on my desk. Stage four. Twenty-eight years old. Every time I think about calling her sister, I just— (My phone’s ringing. Probably the mayor’s office, wanting to know why response times are up again.)” — Priya Narang, EMS DIRECTOR, Uptown (own page, after work, C109)

“To be honest, I've been preoccupied with some tough cases at work lately. It's been weighing on my mind, thinking about what could've been done differently to prevent some of the injuries I've seen. It's not just about the job, it's about the people and their families. I care deeply about my community and it's hard not to take it personally when things don't go as well as they could.” — Priya Narang, EMS DIRECTOR, Uptown (own page, to a reporter, C109)

“Yu’s gonna need a long recovery—those burns were deep, and I’m betting he’s not going back to that job anytime soon. Deacon’s hand—that’s on me. I should’ve pushed harder on the safety protocols. Marcus is healing, but I keep seeing the wreckage in my head, that car folded like paper. And Ariana... I don’t even know how to process that yet. Some days, this job feels like holding water in your hands—no matter how tight your grip, it still slips through.” — Priya Narang, EMS DIRECTOR, Uptown (own page, after work, C110)

“Ariana’s chart is still on my desk. I didn’t mean to bring it home, but it’s stuck in my head—the numbers, the staging, the way her file reads like a countdown. I keep thinking about whether we could’ve caught it sooner, but that’s not how this works and I know it. Deacon’s hand, Maurice’s lungs—some days the board feels like a ledger of things I should’ve pushed harder on. I’ll check in on Marcus in the morning, see if he’s walking yet. For now, it’s just the quiet and the list, and I’m trying to let it sit without picking it apart.” — Priya Narang, EMS DIRECTOR, Uptown (own page, after work, C111)

“Yu Zen’s file is still open on my desk. Twenty-nine years old, Rockridge, and now he’s looking at months of rehab for a hand that might never close right. Deacon’s losing his, I know that much already. Some days I wonder if the board sees the numbers or the people behind them, and I’m too tired to keep fighting that fight tonight. I just keep coming back to the same question: did we get there fast enough, and will it ever feel like we did?” — Priya Narang, EMS DIRECTOR, Uptown (own page, after work, C112)

“The Voices page for this cycle makes me think about accountability because it has my own words on it, and people like Marcus Webb's. Seeing my own reflection on the page alongside others makes me accountable. I want to be able to say that we've done better by the people we're supposed to help. I want to be able to look at cases like Yu Zen's and know we did everything we could.” — Priya Narang, EMS DIRECTOR, Uptown (own page, to a reporter, C112)
“Did we really do everything we could for people like Marcus Webb and Yu Zen?” — Priya Narang, EMS DIRECTOR, Uptown (own page, to a reporter, a question they carry, C112)

“Helena—she's the one I call when the rent's got me twisted or the noise from the street won't let me sleep. She don't sugarcoat, tells me straight when I'm being a damn fool, and I respect that more than I say. Marmol is different—we shared a ladder and a lunch pail on a dozen jobs, but it never went much deeper than that. He'd do a solid if I asked, but I ain't asked, and he ain't offered, and maybe that's just how it is with work people. These days I mostly think about the house, the one I'm clawing toward, and I wonder if either of them would still know me if I finally get it.” — Omar Amici, Construction laborer, Uptown (own page, the night page, C112)
“Will Helena and Marmol still know me if I finally get the house?” — Omar Amici, Construction laborer, Uptown (own page, the night page, a question they carry, C112)

“Helena, I was just thinkin' about you—how you always tell it to me straight. The coffee pot's acting up again, and I swear it's the little things that get under my skin these days. How's your week treating you? Quiet minutes sound like gold right about now. I spent half the weekend staring at for-rent signs, trying to figure out if this neighborhood's still mine or if I'm just a ghost walking through someone else's plans. You always know how to ground a man. Maybe you're right—maybe stickin' around and watchin' is its own kind of work. Mariela says I worry too much, that change comes whether I like it or not, but she's got a point about us still being here.” — Omar Amici, Construction laborer, Uptown (own page, in conversation, C112)

“To be honest, the changes in Uptown have me feeling a bit uneasy. The streets are busier than ever, and it seems like every other place is a for-rent sign these days. I've lived here long enough to see the neighborhood transform, but this feels different. It's like the neighborhood is shifting away from the people who've been here all along. I put on my good suit for Sunday service because some traditions still matter, but walking around, I see more strangers than familiar faces. It's hard not to wonder if this is still my neighborhood or if I'm just a ghost walking through someone else's plans.” — Omar Amici, Construction laborer, Uptown (own page, to a reporter, C112)
“Will the familiar faces who've been here all along still be around, or will it all be strangers?” — Omar Amici, Construction laborer, Uptown (own page, to a reporter, a question they carry, C112)

“Honestly, weekends are always a different animal for us. People aren't commuting, so the whole rhythm shifts. Seeing 12th Street drop the most doesn't surprise me — that station is so tied to the workday crowd and downtown events. When the weekend hits and there's no game or big thing pulling people in, it just goes quiet. We watch these patterns closely because they tell us when to run more trains or when we can give our crews a breather. It's not an anomaly; it's just what a city that lives on weekdays looks like on a Saturday.” — Ximena Mehta, Bart Transit PR, Lake Merritt (own page, to a reporter, C113)

“You know what’s been grating on me? The pile of dirty coffee mugs in the office kitchen. It’s so stupid, but every single day I walk in there and there are like six of them just sitting in the sink, and nobody ever claims them. I’ve got my own stuff to deal with—the rent, the commute, wondering if Deacon remembered to pick up the dry cleaning—and I’m standing there fuming over ceramic and old grounds. Does it actually matter? No. Not one bit. But I think it’s just the little stand-in for everything else that feels out of my control right now. Like, if people can’t even rinse out their own mug, how are we supposed to fix the bigger messes around here? So yeah, I’m worn down, and the mugs are just the thing my brain latched onto.” — Ximena Mehta, Bart Transit PR, Lake Merritt (own page, the midday page, C113)
“How are we supposed to fix the bigger messes around here if we can't even rinse out a mug?” — Ximena Mehta, Bart Transit PR, Lake Merritt (own page, the midday page, a question they carry, C113)

“I've seen more for-rent signs popping up around Uptown, it's like the neighborhood's changing fast. People moving in, people moving out. I don't know Orion Kerkering or Isla Sike personally, but I can relate to the struggle of finding a place to call your own. It's tough out here.” — Omar Amici, Construction laborer, Uptown (own page, to a reporter, C113)
“Will I ever find a place of my own out here, with everyone moving in and out?” — Omar Amici, Construction laborer, Uptown (own page, to a reporter, a question they carry, C113)

“The board’s still up on the wall. Yu Zen, Deacon, Maurice—three names in one week that should have been preventable if the right people gave a damn. I keep going back to Deacon’s hand, how it looked when the crew brought him in. That’s not a wound, that’s a management failure. And Maurice, god, he was coughing blood before we even got the call. Some days I wonder if I’m directing traffic or just counting the bodies after the crash. Ariana’s chart is still on my desk too, folded under a stack of supply orders. I don’t need to look at it again to know what it says. She’s got maybe months, and I keep thinking about how we move heaven and earth for a broken leg but can’t get her a faster scan. The workday’s done. It doesn’t feel like it.” — Priya Narang, EMS DIRECTOR, Uptown (own page, after work, C113)

“The A's winning season is a big deal for us in Uptown. I started a savings jar on the counter to buy season tickets next year, hoping Danny Horn stays in center field. It's not just about the team; when they're doing well, the whole neighborhood feels it. The bars and galleries stay packed, and for a while, it seems like the rent signs disappear. It's a small boost, but it matters. My kids are huge fans, and my husband and I love watching them excited. It's moments like those that make all the stress worth it.” — Priya Narang, EMS DIRECTOR, Uptown (own page, to a reporter, C113)

“Hey, you just get off the late shift? I was about to grab a coffee before heading home—you want to join me for a minute? That left field call's been eating at me too, honestly. Morton's got the ceiling, but Reyna showed he can handle the moment, and that counts for a lot in this town. I just hope whoever they pick doesn't end up second-guessed every single night. You're right about that. Playing here isn't like anywhere else—folks remember every swing, every miss. I've seen guys with all the talent in the world crumble under that. Rosado's got that calm about him, but I keep coming back to Morton. Something about his fire reminds me of the old days.” — Ximena Mehta, Bart Transit PR, Lake Merritt (own page, in conversation, C113)
